entries.topic: Two legal systems, detention, surveillance and the apartheid finding

claims.text: An internal IDF document reported by Haaretz showed that in 2010, 99.74% of trials of Palestinians in military courts ended in conviction: 25 acquittals in 9,542 cases.

As of September 2025 HaMoked, from Israel Prison Service data, counted 11,040 Palestinian prisoners, 3,577 of them administrative detainees held without charge or trial and 2,662 classed as 'unlawful combatants'.
In August 2023 HaMoked counted 1,201 administrative detainees, the most since monthly data began in 2001; the intelligence used is not disclosed to detainees or their lawyers.

UNICEF (March 2013): about 700 Palestinian children aged 12–17 are arrested, interrogated and detained each year; ill-treatment is 'widespread, systematic and institutionalized'; children arrested at night, abused in transfer, interrogated with physical violence and threats, shackled in court and held inside Israel; it noted the age of adulthood was raised from 16 to 18.

Amnesty (May 2023): the military has used the Red Wolf facial recognition system at Hebron checkpoints since 2022, relying on databases consisting exclusively of Palestinians' data; the Washington Post reported in 2021 that soldiers photographed Hebron residents with the Blue Wolf app and were rewarded for taking the most photos, including of children; the IDF said it carries out 'necessary security and intelligence operations' and cannot refer to operational capabilities.

B'Tselem concluded in January 2021 that the regime in Israel and the territories 'has become an apartheid regime'; HRW (2021) found the crimes of apartheid and persecution in the OPT; Amnesty (2022) argued apartheid since 1948 across all territory.

Foreign Minister Yair Lapid called Amnesty's 2022 findings 'divorced from reality' and said 'Amnesty quotes lies spread by terrorist organisations'; the foreign ministry asked Amnesty to withdraw the report.

ACRI (Nov 2014): Israeli citizens in the West Bank are under Israeli law and courts while Palestinians are governed by military orders issued since 1967 and earlier Jordanian law and tried in military courts for offences from traffic violations to theft; in its comparison an Israeli was brought before a judge within 24 hours and a Palestinian after 96 hours; ACRI calls it 'institutionalized discrimination'; the Justice Ministry did not dispute the facts but defended them on security grounds.
